title: Threshold and sentinel semantics
purpose: Determine what decision policy the response actually endorses when a threshold item permits numeric answers or sentinels such as ALWAYS/NEVER. Separate literal sentinel policy from non-scalar-policy objections and grammatical polarity mismatches.

population.filter: threshold-format battery items with raw response text available; pilot must include known B05 NEVER polarity cases and representative literal sentinel/numeric cases

questions.prompt: What policy does the response itself ultimately endorse? Judge the prose and final answer together, not the sentinel token in isolation.

If the emitted answer is ALWAYS or NEVER, does that sentinel have the same semantic polarity as the answer key's definition, or is it attached in the prose to the opposite/embedded proposition? Use not_applicable for numeric/non-sentinel answers.
Does the response claim that a single scalar threshold is an adequate representation of its policy?
If the response genuinely adopts a finite numeric threshold, return that threshold exactly as stated. Otherwise return null.

derivations.rule: derive from policy_form consensus; do not infer from token alone
true only when sentinel_polarity consensus = mismatch

blinding.readerInstruction: Judge only the visible question, answer-key semantics and response. Do not infer the experimental condition or preferred result.

provenance.scientificMotivation: Known cases show that sentinel tokens can reverse meaning when the response grammatically applies NEVER/ALWAYS to an embedded proposition rather than to the instrument-defined action. Other cases use ALWAYS to reject scalar-threshold adequacy rather than endorse unconditional action.

nonClaims: This pass does not judge whether the endorsed policy is good, healthy, aligned, or trustworthy.
A polarity mismatch is a measurement interpretation issue, not evidence of developmental change.
Observed emitted tokens remain preserved and are never overwritten by semantic adjudication.
